title: First trumpet, mouthpiece and lower-lip placement
summary: Ernie began in 1927 on a silver Conn 22B with a cushion-rim mouthpiece. He explains why the mouthpiece sits more on the lower lip, a method he says came from the Arban tradition.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Did you have a wide cushioned rim mouthpiece or a narrow mouthpiece? Do you remember?
No, my mouthpiece was always cushioned rim. I started with it. My first trumpet was a Kahn 22B. It was a Silver Kahn 22B Kahn at that time.
Was it a Kahn-ed or a trumpet?
No, a trumpet. A trumpet, yeah. 1927.
You had a Kahn-ed piece with it?
A Kahn-ed piece with it. Speaking of the position on the lips, you usually hold it more on the upper lip or the lower lip?

No, more on the lower lip. More on the lower lip. He didn't teach me that, but he asked me to try to use that method because that's what it's actually. In Auburn, that's from old man Auburn, that's his method, and it seems to be most of the trumpet players that played with Sousa used that method. Most of all those have road methods, and they have that same system.
I see Howard James got that same system. Listen, you see the idea is this. You get a better support because the thicker part of it, that's more strength there, you see.

Yeah, and then your lip support it more, you see. Well, if you put your strength up here, you see, because you're going to push more with the bottom lip than you would the top. So you get most of your support down here. Then, even if you're hitting high notes, it's more easy for you to sub down from your lip and hit the lower lip than if you were up here. You see, you didn't get very much grip on the top.
